Which offices decide what a Pennsylvania house owes in property tax?

Two steps produce every bill. A county assessment office puts a value on each parcel, and then the county, the municipality and the school district apply their rates to that value. Chapter 88 of Title 53 governs the first step. It tells the assessor to work from an established predetermined ratio that cannot exceed 100 percent of actual value, and the county commissioners adopt that ratio by ordinance.

Since every county chooses its own ratio and every taxing body its own rate, identical homes can carry unlike bills from one corner of the state to another. A seller should look at the bill for the specific parcel, which the county assessment office or the local tax collector can supply, rather than at averages for the region.

How is a Pennsylvania home valued for tax?

Section 8842 makes the assessor weigh three methods together: the cost approach, the comparable sales approach and the income approach. A sale price in the base year or the current year counts as evidence but does not control, and it can be adjusted up or down to match similar property in the county. A county may use current market value or adopt a base-year market value.

So a fresh sale price is one input among several. Section 8843 adds a guardrail: the assessment office may not engage in spot reassessment of single properties. An owner who is subjected to it may appeal on that issue and, if the board or a court agrees, recover taxes paid with interest. A changed assessment that results from a normal appeal does not count as spot reassessment.

What is the deadline to appeal an assessment?

The default filing date is September 1. County commissioners may pick a different date, no earlier than August 1, if they publish notice at least two weeks ahead. Anyone aggrieved by an assessment may file, even if the figure did not change from the year before. A new assessment or a mid-year change comes with its own clock: the mailed notice must say an appeal can be filed within 40 days of the notice date.

  • Put the appeal in writing and name the appellant, the parcel address, the owner, the assessment at issue and where to mail the hearing notice.
  • The board hears annual appeals and acts on them by October 31.
  • It mails hearing notices at least 20 days before the hearing, and a no-show is presumed to have abandoned the case.
  • At the hearing the board finds market value as of the filing date and applies the ratio, unless the state's published common level ratio differs from the county ratio by more than 15 percent.

Either side may then take the board's decision to the common pleas court of the county. A lowered assessment generally starts working in the taxing district's next fiscal year, which makes an appeal slow relief for anyone about to sell.

What relief programs lower the bill for owners?

Two state programs matter. The homestead and farmstead exclusion cuts the assessed value of a qualifying primary residence by a uniform amount before school tax is figured. The Property Tax/Rent Rebate Program sends cash back to eligible older residents and people with disabilities.

Pennsylvania property tax relief programs (Department of Community and Economic Development; Department of Revenue)
ProgramWho qualifiesKey rule
Homestead or farmstead exclusionOwner-occupied primary residenceApply by March 1 before the tax year; file with the county assessment office
Property Tax/Rent RebateAge 65 and older, widows and widowers 50 and older, people with disabilities 18 and olderHousehold income of $48,110 or less; rebates from $380 to $1,000

The rebate shrinks as income rises: the top tier is $1,000 for income up to $8,550, and the bottom tier is $380 for income between $19,241 and $48,110. Owners with $32,070 or less in income whose property taxes exceed 15 percent of income can receive a supplement of $190 to $500, and so can residents of Philadelphia, Scranton and Pittsburgh. The 2025 claim year carried a December 31, 2026 filing deadline, and later years set their own, so read the department's program page before filing.

How does the homestead exclusion work?

The Taxpayer Relief Act, Act 1 of Special Session 1 of 2006, sends state money to school districts, which then lower the assessed value of homesteads and farmsteads. A homestead is a dwelling used mainly as the domicile of an owner who is a natural person. A farmstead means the buildings on a farm of at least ten contiguous acres where an owner lives. Owners have no guarantee of an exclusion unless funding exists.

An application filed by March 1 covers the tax year that follows, whether it begins July 1 or January 1. By December 31, a school district must notify an owner whose property was not approved or whose approval is about to lapse. The March 1 date is in section 341 of Act 72 of 2004, so the Governor cannot move it alone. Request the county form from the assessment office and ask how a sale affects the exclusion on file.

Who is billed when the owner has died?

Section 8863 lets the county assess a decedent's property under the dead owner's name or under the personal representative's name while it stays in the estate. A bill addressed to a deceased owner is therefore ordinary, and the estate still owes it. The personal representative pays from estate funds while the house waits for a buyer.

After letters issue, an heir should ask the county assessment office to update the mailing address and to report what happens to any exclusion on file. The law defines a homestead by use as an owner's domicile, and a house left empty after a death may no longer fit that definition.

What property tax steps come with selling a house?

Section 8862.1 puts a duty on the buyer: register the deed with the county's chief assessor within 30 days of conveyance, unless the deed was already recorded with the recorder of deeds. A willful failure is a summary offense carrying a fine of $50 to $100.

The realty transfer tax is its own charge. Pennsylvania takes one percent of the value on a transfer by deed, county recorders collect it along with any local levy, and buyer and seller answer for it jointly. The recorder in the house's county can quote the local portion.

  • Request the latest bill and any unpaid balance on the parcel from the tax collector.
  • Have the title company explain how school and county taxes will be split at closing.
  • Check with the assessment office whether a homestead exclusion sits on file in the seller's name.

When taxes are behind, call the county tax claim bureau for a payoff figure and ask whether the parcel has been given a sale date.

Frequently asked questions

When must I file a Pennsylvania assessment appeal?

By September 1, unless the county commissioners picked an earlier date no sooner than August 1. A new or changed assessment carries a separate 40 day window counted from the notice date.

Does a new sale price raise my assessment?

It can be weighed, but section 8842 says the price is not controlling and may be revised to match similar property. A county may also adopt a base-year market value, which the statute allows.

What is the homestead exclusion deadline?

March 1 before the tax year, filed with the county assessment office. The exclusion covers only a primary residence.

Who registers a new deed with the assessor?

The buyer, within 30 days of conveyance, unless the deed was already recorded with the recorder of deeds. A willful failure is a summary offense under 53 Pa.C.S. 8862.1.

Is there a state rebate on property tax for seniors?

Yes. The Property Tax/Rent Rebate Program pays $380 to $1,000 to eligible homeowners and renters who are 65 or older, widowed at 50 or older, or disabled at 18 or older, with household income of $48,110 or less.

How does Pennsylvania inheritance tax work when you inherit a house?

Pennsylvania levies an inheritance tax on property that passes at death, and the closer the heir's family tie, the lower the rate. A house is valued like any other asset, so an heir who keeps it, rents it or sells it still sits inside the same tax calculation. The Department of Revenue describes the tax as a percentage of the value of a decedent's estate transferred to beneficiaries by will, to heirs by intestacy and to transferees by operation of law.

The tax is a Pennsylvania matter separate from the federal system and separate from the realty transfer tax that applies when a deed changes hands for a price. Heirs who plan to sell should keep three questions apart: what the estate owes the state, who has authority to sign a deed, and what the buyer's closing will cost. This page covers the first and touches the other two.

What are the Pennsylvania inheritance tax rates by heir?

The state sets four rates, from zero up to fifteen percent. The department's overview page lists them as follows.

Pennsylvania inheritance tax rates by relationship to the decedent (Department of Revenue, Inheritance Tax overview)
Who receives the propertyRate
Surviving spouse, or a parent receiving from a child aged 21 or younger0 percent
Direct descendants and lineal heirs4.5 percent
Siblings12 percent
Other heirs15 percent

Charitable organizations, exempt institutions and government entities are exempt. Property that spouses owned jointly is also exempt from inheritance tax.

Two narrower exemptions matter for real estate. Certain farm land and other agricultural property is exempt for decedents who died after June 30, 2012, when it goes to eligible recipients. Personal property from the estate of a service member who died from an injury or illness received on active duty is exempt for deaths on or after September 6, 2022. The department points to Inheritance Tax Informational Notice 2012-01 for the farm rules.

When is the tax due, and what is the three month discount?

The tax is due on the date of death and becomes delinquent nine months later. If it is paid within three months of death, the state allows a 5 percent discount. Both rules come from the Department of Revenue's overview and payment pages.

For a house, the discount creates a timing choice. An heir who can pay quickly saves five percent of the tax, but an estate that holds mostly real estate may have little cash in the first ninety days. Selling the house early can fund the payment, which is one reason heirs ask about a fast sale. If the estate cannot pay in full, the department's payment page describes payment plans and tells taxpayers who cannot pay in full to contact the department.

  • Pennsylvania residents pay through the Register of Wills in the county where the decedent lived.
  • Non-residents pay the Department of Revenue directly.
  • Plan the sale date around the nine month mark, since delinquency starts then.

Who signs the deed to sell an inherited house?

The personal representative signs, after the Register of Wills grants letters. Under 20 Pa.C.S. 3351, a personal representative may sell real property not specifically devised, and may sell specifically devised property with the joinder of the devisee. Unless the will says otherwise, that sale can be public or private.

Where the will denies the power to sell, or where it is advisable that a sale have the effect of a judicial sale, section 3353 sends the request to the orphans' court division of the county that granted letters. A buyer then receives clear title under section 3357, which passes the decedent's full title free of legacy liens and estate debts if the representative gave any bond the law requires. Ask the title company which documents it needs before it will insure the deed.

The same title adds a paperwork duty that touches tax: under section 3301(c), the personal representative files the inventory by the date the account is filed or the due date, with extensions, for the inheritance tax return, whichever comes first.

Does the realty transfer tax apply to an inherited house?

Handing a house to an heir through a will or intestacy escapes the realty transfer tax. A later sale to a buyer is a different event, because a deed for a price falls under the tax. The department's page names property passed by testate or intestate succession among the exempt transfers.

The commonwealth takes one percent of the value on a transfer by deed. Recorders of Deeds in each county gather it along with any local add-on and forward the state portion. Seller and buyer are jointly and severally liable, so ask the closing agent how the charge will be settled. The local add-on differs by place, and the recorder's office in the house's county can quote it.

Who inherits the house when there is no will?

Intestacy rules in 20 Pa.C.S. 2102 and 2103 decide it, and the answer also sets each person's tax rate. With no children and no surviving parent, a spouse receives everything. Where all of the decedent's children are also the spouse's children, the spouse gets the first $30,000 plus half of what remains, and the children share the other half.

When some children come from a different relationship, the spouse's share drops to half of the intestate estate. Where several heirs share a house, each heir's slice is taxed at the rate for that heir's relationship, so one sale can involve more than one percentage. Ask the Register of Wills to confirm the heirs on the petition before anyone signs a listing agreement.

What changed for estates with no family heirs?

Act 50 of 2025 changed who inherits when no relatives exist. Before January 16, 2026, the Commonwealth was the first statutory heir in that situation. The law now sends the estate first to an endowed community fund in the decedent's municipality, then in the school district, then in the county, and only after those the Commonwealth.

This matters to a distant relative or a friend named nowhere in a will: the question of who qualifies as an heir sits ahead of any tax rate. The order of succession itself is in 20 Pa.C.S. 2103, which runs from issue to parents, to the issue of the parents, to grandparents and then to more remote lines.

What should an heir do before listing the house?

Work through the steps in order, because each one unlocks the next.

  • Confirm that letters have been granted by the Register of Wills in the county of the decedent's last principal residence.
  • Ask the Register of Wills what value documentation the inheritance tax return needs for the house.
  • Decide whether to pay within three months for the 5 percent discount.
  • Ask the title company whether the sale needs the joinder of a specific devisee.
  • Ask the county Recorder of Deeds for the local transfer tax rate and recording fees.

A cash buyer can close without repairs or showings, which helps when an estate is paying carrying costs on an empty house. The estate still needs letters, a signing representative and tax payment planning before closing.

Frequently asked questions

Do I owe inheritance tax if I inherit my parent's house in Pennsylvania?

Yes, at 4.5 percent of the value you receive, because a child is a direct descendant. The surviving spouse pays 0 percent. A sibling pays 12 percent and other heirs pay 15 percent.

Is there a discount for paying early?

Yes. The Department of Revenue allows a 5 percent discount if the tax is paid within three months of the date of death. After nine months the tax is delinquent.

Where do I pay inheritance tax for a Pennsylvania resident?

You pay the Register of Wills in the county where the decedent lived. Payments for non-residents go to the Department of Revenue instead.

Can I sell the inherited house before the tax is paid?

Yes, if the personal representative holds letters and the title company is satisfied, and the tax can be paid from the estate or from sale proceeds. Ask the title company how it wants that handled at closing.

Is the property I inherit taxed twice when I sell it?

No. The inheritance tax applies once to the transfer at death. A sale later adds the realty transfer tax, which is 1 percent at the state level plus any local rate, and succession itself is exempt from that tax.

Pennsylvania homeowners apply for the homestead exclusion with their county, and the benefit reduces the assessed value used for school taxes.

What is the Pennsylvania homestead exclusion?

It is a reduction in the assessed value of a primary residence, applied before school property tax is calculated. The Department of Community and Economic Development explains that the Taxpayer Relief Act, Act 1 of Special Session 1 of 2006, signed on June 27, 2006, sends property tax reduction allocations to each school district, and the district passes the benefit through a homestead or farmstead exclusion.

Every qualifying homestead or farmstead in the district is reduced by the same amount. Only a primary residence is eligible, and most owner-occupied homes and farms can qualify. The state is also clear that homeowners are not guaranteed the exclusion unless an added income tax is approved by voter referendum or enough funds have been collected for the Commonwealth to make the allocations.

Which properties count as a homestead?

A homestead is a dwelling, with its parcel and other improvements, that an owner who is a natural person uses as a domicile. The statutory definition quoted by DCED has three branches.

  • A house or other dwelling primarily used as the domicile of an owner who is a natural person. The land is left out if someone else owns the land under the dwelling.
  • A condominium or cooperative unit used as the domicile of a natural person who owns it, limited to the assessed value of that unit.
  • A dwelling where only part is used as the owner's domicile, in which case the homestead is the share of the property equal to that portion.

A farmstead is a different category: the buildings and structures on a farm of at least ten contiguous acres that are used mainly for commercial agriculture, and it applies only to farms that serve as an owner's domicile.

When is the application due?

For tax years that begin July 1 or January 1, the application must be filed by the preceding March 1. DCED adds that school districts must notify homeowners by December 31 each year if a property has not been approved or if its approval is about to expire, so a letter in late December is a signal to refile.

The March 1 date comes from Section 341 of Act 72 of 2004, and DCED states that the Governor cannot extend it by executive order. Only new legislation could change it. Forms come from the county assessment office, so call the assessor in the county where the house sits for the current application.

How do the state, Allegheny County and Philadelphia programs differ?

The statewide exclusion lowers school taxes, while other homestead programs come from local law. Allegheny County runs a separate Act 50 exclusion that applies to county tax purposes only. Philadelphia runs its own Homestead Exemption through its Department of Revenue, with a flat $100,000 reduction and a December 1 filing date.

Three homestead programs and their filing rules (sources: DCED, Allegheny County, City of Philadelphia)
ProgramWhat it reducesFiling date
State exclusion under Act 1 of 2006Assessed value used for school property taxMarch 1 before the tax year
Allegheny County Act 50 exclusionAssessment for Allegheny County tax onlySet by the county; ask Allegheny County Real Estate
Philadelphia Homestead Exemption$100,000 off the taxable assessed valueDecember 1 each year; October 1 for the bill to reflect it

What is Act 50 and who can use it?

Act 50 of 1998 lets local governments create their own homestead and farmstead exclusions. Allegheny County explains that Pennsylvania voters approved a constitutional change in November 1997 to allow a homestead exclusion, the General Assembly passed the Homestead Property Exclusion Program Act in May 1998, and the Act was amended on October 31, 2000.

Under the law, school districts, counties, townships, boroughs and cities can each adopt an exclusion. A taxing body can do so without changing its tax structure, as long as it can cover the cost without raising real property taxes. Districts that shift toward an earned income tax and lower the real property tax must use the exclusions to deliver the cut, and in exchange they drop several small taxes such as the per capita, occupation and occupational privilege taxes.

  • County of the second class: Act 50 as amended lets the county adopt its own rules and procedures for the program in place of the usual state administrative section.
  • Other locations: ask the county assessor whether the school district, county or municipality has adopted an exclusion of its own.
  • Amounts: each taxing body sets its own figure, so a neighbor in a different district may see a different reduction.

What does Philadelphia require and allow?

Philadelphia says you qualify if you own the home and live in it as your primary residence, and a mortgage or delinquent taxes do not disqualify you. Most homeowners save up to $1,399 a year on the Real Estate Tax bill, according to the City, and approval carries forward each year while you keep owning and living in the property.

  • You reapply only if the deed changes, for example when you refinance or add or remove a co-owner.
  • Owners with a 10-year residential tax abatement are not eligible until it expires, and a removed abatement cannot be put back.
  • A conditional exemption of up to three years is available when your name is not on the deed, such as after an inheritance, a fraudulent deed or a rent-to-own purchase.
  • Applications can go through the Philadelphia Tax Center, by phone at (215) 686-9200, or by mail to the Department of Revenue.

A denial can be appealed to the Board of Revision of Taxes within 30 days of the date on the denial letter. If a property no longer qualifies, the owner must tell Revenue within 45 days.

What happens to the exclusion when you sell the house?

The benefit follows an owner who lives in the home, so a sale ends your claim and the buyer applies on a new deed. Philadelphia asks for a fresh application when the deed changes, so a new owner who plans to live there should file once the deed is recorded.

Property tax bills do not stop at settlement. Ask the county treasurer or tax claim office which installments are paid, and check with your settlement agent how the closing statement divides the current bill. If you stop living in the house before you sell, for example after moving out of an inherited home, tell the assessor, because the exclusion applies only to a primary residence. In Philadelphia an owner who stops qualifying has 45 days to notify Revenue.

What should a seller check before listing a Pennsylvania home?

Start with the assessment office record for your parcel and confirm whether an exclusion is on it. If none is listed and you live in the house, ask the assessor how the county treats a late filing, since the March 1 date is fixed by statute for the following tax year.

Next, ask the county treasurer for the current tax bill and the payment status of each installment, so the closing statement divides the bill correctly. If the house was inherited and the deed still names a deceased relative, Philadelphia's conditional exemption shows that title problems are recognized in the program, and the county assessor can say what proof applies where you are.

Finally, gather the paperwork a title company will ask for: the most recent school and county tax bills, any homestead approval letter, and any abatement papers. Having them ready keeps a small tax question from delaying settlement.

Frequently asked questions

Is the Pennsylvania homestead exclusion automatic?

No, you apply to the county assessment office, and the application must be filed by March 1 before the tax year begins. School districts notify owners by December 31 if a property is not approved or its approval is expiring.

Does a rental or second home qualify?

No, only a primary residence is eligible. A dwelling must be used as the domicile of an owner who is a natural person, and when only part of the dwelling is the owner's home, the homestead is limited to that part.

Can Pennsylvania extend the March 1 deadline?

No executive order can do it. DCED states that the March 1 date is set by Section 341 of Act 72 of 2004, and the Governor cannot extend it, so only a change in the law could move the date.

How much does the Philadelphia Homestead Exemption save?

It removes $100,000 from the assessed value used to compute Real Estate Tax, and the City says most homeowners save up to $1,399 a year. The final filing date is December 1, with October 1 recommended for early filers.

Who do I ask for the form in another county?

Ask the county assessment office. DCED says the county provides its own homestead and farmstead application, and the filing dates and amounts for your school district come from that office.

Who qualifies for the Pennsylvania Property Tax/Rent Rebate?

Pennsylvania homeowners and renters qualify when they fit one of three age or disability groups and keep household income at or under $48,110 a year. The Department of Revenue runs the program, and gaming revenue pays for it.

  • Adults 65 and older.
  • Widows and widowers 50 and older.
  • People with disabilities 18 and older.

The income cap rose under Act 7 of 2023, which the Department says brought nearly 175,000 more people into eligibility. The program began in 1971, and the Department reports that older and disabled adults have received over $9.2 billion in property tax and rent relief since then.

How much does the rebate pay at each income level?

A standard rebate runs from $380 to $1,000, and the amount falls as household income rises. Four income bands set the payment.

Most claimants land in the widest band, because it spans everything from $19,241 up to the $48,110 cap. A household at the top of that band still receives the $380 rebate.

What is the supplemental rebate, and who gets it?

The supplement adds $190 to $500 on top of the standard rebate for applicants with the greatest need, and the Department figures it automatically from the claim. Two groups can receive it.

  • Property owners with income of $32,070 or less whose property taxes are more than 15% of that income.
  • Applicants who live in Philadelphia, Scranton or Pittsburgh.

Stacked on the standard rebate, the supplement lifts the top payment to $1,500 in the lowest income band. The next bands reach $1,155 and $690, and the band from $19,241 to $32,070 reaches $570. Nobody files a separate form for the supplement.

Which documents prove age, income and taxes paid?

The claim needs four kinds of proof: age, income, tax or rent paid, and the school district code for your county. The Department accepts photocopies for age.

  • Age: a birth certificate, driver's license or PA identification card, passport, Medicare card, PACE or PACENET card, hospital birth record, church baptismal record, or military or naturalization papers that show age.
  • Homeowners: receipted tax bills for the year being claimed.
  • Renters: a rent certificate filled in by the landlord or the landlord's agent. If the landlord's signature cannot be obtained, a rent certificate with a notarized affidavit works.
  • Income records for the claim year.

When a lender pays your bill from escrow, ask your local tax collector's office for a receipted copy. Keep these records with the claim, since the same set is needed again each year.

Which extra schedules go with the PA-1000 claim?

Most applicants file only the PA-1000, but several situations call for an added schedule. The Department lists them on its forms page.

  • PA-1000 RC: renters.
  • PA-1000 A: someone who owned more than one home during the year, or an applicant who has died.
  • PA-1000 B/D/E: a widow or widower aged 50 to 64 who remarried, a renter who receives cash public assistance, or an owner who ran a business or rented out part of the home.
  • PA-1000 F/G: more than one eligible person on the deed or lease, or a deceased applicant.
  • PA-1000 PS: a physician's confirmation of permanent and total disability.
  • DEX-41: a claim filed for someone who has died.

Estates that are getting a Pennsylvania house ready for sale often meet the last three items, because a parent or spouse may have died before the claim was filed.

When is the deadline, and when do rebates go out?

The deadline for the 2025 claim year is December 31, 2026, and an application postmarked by that day is accepted. Later claim years carry their own deadline, which the Department posts on its program page.

The payment calendar follows the same pattern each cycle. Automated calls confirming receipt begin in April, and calls confirming approval begin in June. Rebates start going out July 1 by direct deposit or mailed check, whichever you chose on the application.

You can file online through mypath.pa.gov, by mail, or in person. Hundreds of in-person help sites around the state assist with the form at no charge.

What would a few sample households receive?

The tables above combine in predictable ways, so a quick check shows roughly where a household lands. These examples use only the Department's published bands and maximums.

  • A 70-year-old homeowner in a Pennsylvania borough with $9,500 of income sits in the $770 band, so the standard maximum is $770. Living outside Philadelphia, Scranton and Pittsburgh, the supplement applies only if property tax exceeds 15% of income.
  • A 67-year-old renter in Scranton with $14,000 of income sits in the same $770 band, and the Scranton supplement can add up to $385, for a ceiling of $1,155.
  • A 58-year-old widow in Pittsburgh with $30,000 of income sits in the $380 band, and the supplement can add up to $190, for a ceiling of $570.
  • A disabled adult of 45 with $44,000 of income sits in the $380 band and, above the $32,070 supplement limit, receives no supplement.

The rebate is a maximum. The Department calculates the final figure from the claim, so use these examples to judge whether filing is worth your time. For most households at or under the cap, it is.

What happens to a claim after I file it?

A filed claim passes through three public milestones: a receipt call in April, an approval call in June, and payment beginning July 1. Those calls are automated, and they reach applicants by phone.

The Department compares your age or disability category, income and tax or rent figure with the documents you attach. A disability claim also needs the physician's PA-1000 PS confirmation that the condition is permanent and total, so ask your doctor for it early.

Payment goes out in the form you picked on the application, either direct deposit or a mailed check. If your address or bank details change between years, correct them on the next application.

How do I check my status and avoid scam calls?

Call the Department of Revenue at 1-888-PATAXES (728-2937) to check a claim, or use the online status tool. Have the primary applicant's Social Security number, date of birth and claim year ready. General program questions go to 1-888-222-9190.

Past applicants have received calls from scammers. The Department states it will never ask for bank account information by phone, and callers who do should be reported to the Office of Attorney General.

Do I have to reapply for the rebate every year?

Yes. If you still meet the rules, you must file a new application each year, because the amount depends on that year's income and the tax or rent you paid. Past applicants usually receive a booklet or reminder letter in the mail.

What is the most a Pennsylvania resident can receive?

The standard rebate tops out at $1,000. With the supplement, the lowest income band can reach $1,500, and that applies to owners meeting the 15% tax-to-income test or people living in Philadelphia, Scranton or Pittsburgh.

Can renters get the rebate?

Yes. Renters file the PA-1000 with Schedule RC, which carries a rent certificate from the landlord. A notarized affidavit replaces the landlord's signature when it cannot be obtained.

Can someone claim the rebate for a person who has died?

Yes. A claim for a deceased applicant uses form DEX-41 together with Schedule A or F/G, depending on the situation. An estate's representative should read the form instructions before filing.

How does Pennsylvania treat a quitclaim deed for tax purposes?

Pennsylvania taxes a quitclaim deed the same way it taxes any other deed whenever real estate actually changes hands. The regulation at 61 Pa. Code 91.164 says a quitclaim is taxable on the same basis as another deed if there is an actual conveyance.

The state realty transfer tax is 1% of the value of the real estate, including contracted-for improvements, and it applies to deeds, instruments, long-term leases and other writings. Grantor and grantee are both liable for it, and the regulation lets them split the payment however they agree without limiting the Commonwealth's rights against either one.

County Recorders of Deeds collect the tax when a document is filed for recording. Many counties add local realty transfer tax, and municipalities and school districts may share that local portion.

What does a quitclaim transfer cost in a real county?

The total depends on the local rate set where the property sits. Allegheny County publishes two worked examples for a $40,000 house that show how far the total can swing.

Realty transfer tax on a $40,000 sale in Allegheny County, from the county's Realty Transfer Taxes page
LocationStateLocalTotal
Shaler Township1% ($400)0.5% township and 0.5% school district ($400)2% ($800)
City of Pittsburgh1% ($400)3% city and 1% school district ($1,600)5% ($2,000)

The county says its combined rate runs from 2% to 5% of the consideration, with 1% going to the state. Ask the recorder of deeds in your own county for the local rates before you sign a deed.

Which quitclaim transfers are excluded from the tax?

Pennsylvania excludes a long list of transfers, and several of them show up in everyday quitclaims between relatives and in estate work. The Department of Revenue says transfers among certain family members and property passed by will or intestate succession are exempt.

Section 91.193 of the regulations gives the detail. Among the exclusions:

  • Transfers between spouses, between a parent or grandparent and a child or grandchild, and between siblings.
  • A transfer between an individual and a sibling's spouse, unless the sibling has died and that spouse has remarried.
  • Transfers between former spouses when the property was acquired by either of them before or during the marriage.
  • A transfer for no or nominal consideration from a personal representative to an heir or devisee.
  • A deed in lieu of foreclosure to a mortgage holder on a bona fide mortgage in default.
  • Any transaction where the true value of the interest is $100 or less.

Two limits matter. A new transfer by the recipient within one year is taxed as if the original grantor had made it to the final buyer, and a decedent's estate does not count as a family member for the family exclusion.

When is a confirmatory or correctional deed not taxable?

A deed given without consideration only to confirm title under an earlier recorded document is not taxable, and that includes a deed that simply records a transfer by survivorship. Section 91.152 attaches three conditions.

  • The grantee already holds record title under a prior deed.
  • The deed exists solely to make that record title secure.
  • The grantor either has no interest in the property or received it through a document that was void from the start.

If a quitclaim moves ownership to a new person or entity, those conditions fail and the 1% applies. Section 91.193 also lists correctional deeds among the excluded transactions, and the Department's regulations on correctional deeds (section 91.151) set their conditions, so read that section before relying on it.

Do I need a statement of value with the deed?

Often yes. Anyone claiming an exclusion must show the true, full and complete value of the property on a statement of value, form REV-183. Two exceptions apply under 61 Pa. Code 91.194: familial transfers and public utility easements. For those, the statement can just explain why the document is not taxable.

Allegheny County adds that a REV-183 is required when the deed lists no consideration or when certain exemptions are claimed. For a family transfer, the county accepts a statement on the deed such as a note that it is a familial transfer exempt from realty transfer tax. Other counties set their own habits, so ask the recorder before the deed is signed.

What else must a Pennsylvania deed include to be recorded?

The recorder in each county screens deeds for form as well as tax. Allegheny County's published guidelines give a useful picture of what a recorder looks for.

  • A complete legal description naming the municipality, the county and state, plus a recorded lot number with plan book reference, a metes and bounds description, or a prior deed reference.
  • The parcel identification number on every deed.
  • Matching worded and numeric consideration on the deed.
  • A Certificate of Residence with typed tax-bill and owner mailing addresses, or the same information inside the deed.
  • A separate check for transfer tax and another for recording fees.

The county rejects deeds with invalid mailing addresses, and an incorrect deed may need a corrective deed filed later. Its recorder will answer recording questions but will not decide whether a deed is legally correct, which is a question for your attorney.

Where does the transfer tax money go?

The Commonwealth keeps the 1% state share, and the Recorders of Deeds remit it to the Department of Revenue. Most of it is deposited in the General Fund, and 15% of collections go to the Keystone Recreation, Park and Conservation Fund.

Local rates are separate from the state 1%. Allegheny County keeps a rate list by municipality and school district, and its two examples above show a 2% total in Shaler Township against 5% in Pittsburgh. Because the county collects state and local shares in one transaction, a single deed can send money to the Commonwealth, a municipality and a school district.

Can a quitclaim deed help me sell a Pennsylvania house?

A quitclaim is one way to put record title in the name of the person who will sign the sale contract, and each such step is taxed under the rules above. Recorded deeds form the chain a buyer's closing agent will review, so a deed that the recorder rejects can delay the closing date.

Family transfers before a sale deserve extra care. The exclusion for a parent and child holds only for the transfer itself, and the one-year look-through can bring a tax bill if the child resells quickly.

Before you sign, confirm three things with the county recorder and your attorney: whether an exclusion truly fits, which local rate applies, and what the recorder wants on the page. The one-year rule on later transfers can also change the tax if the property is sold soon after a family transfer.

Frequently asked questions

Does a quitclaim deed avoid Pennsylvania transfer tax?

No. A quitclaim is taxed like any other deed when real estate actually changes hands. Only the listed exclusions, such as certain family transfers, remove the tax.

Is a transfer to my child taxed?

Generally no. Transfers between a parent or grandparent and a child or grandchild are on the exclusion list. If the child sells the property within one year, that later sale is taxed as if the parent were selling.

Who pays the realty transfer tax?

Grantor and grantee share legal responsibility for the 1% state tax. They may agree between themselves who pays, but the Commonwealth can pursue either one.

Do I always need a REV-183 statement of value?

Not always. Familial transfers and public utility easements can use a short explanation instead of the full value. Most other exclusions require the true, full value on the form.

Where do I record a Pennsylvania deed?

File it with the Recorder of Deeds in the county where the property sits. That office collects state and local transfer tax and the recording fee, usually as separate payments.

What happens before a Pennsylvania sheriff sale can be held?

No sheriff sale of real property can go forward until the plaintiff files an affidavit with the sheriff and the required notice has been served. Pa.R.C.P. 3129.1 sets that rule, and it applies to a sale held on a writ of execution after a judgment.

The affidavit lists, as best the plaintiff knows, the owner or reputed owner, the defendant in the judgment, every person holding a record lien, and anyone with a record interest the sale could affect. It also names people with an unrecorded interest of which the plaintiff has knowledge. If an address cannot be found, the affidavit says so.

What notices must an owner receive?

Three separate notices precede the sale: handbills, written notice and newspaper publication. Pa.R.C.P. 3129.2 sets the timing for each one.

Notice of sale of real property, summarized from Pa.R.C.P. 3129.2
NoticeWho gives itTiming
HandbillsSheriff, posted at the sheriff's office and on the propertyAt least 30 days before the sale
Written noticePlaintiff, to everyone named in the affidavitServed at least 30 days before the sale
Newspaper publicationSheriff, once a week for three weeksFirst notice at least 21 days before the sale

Each handbill describes the property and its improvements, the judgment, the owner's name, and the time and place of the sale. It also tells claimants that the sheriff will file a schedule of distribution within 30 days after the sale, and that objections to it are due within ten days of filing.

How is the written notice delivered?

The method depends on who the recipient is. The plaintiff prepares the notice, and the rule allows several routes.

  • An owner or a defendant who has not appeared in the case: service by the sheriff or a competent adult, or by the plaintiff mailing a copy under Rule 403.
  • A defendant who has appeared: service by the plaintiff under Rule 440.
  • Other people named in the affidavit: ordinary mail from the plaintiff, backed by a USPS Form 3817 certificate of mailing. Service is complete on mailing, and returned mail does not undo it.
  • If neither personal service nor mailing works: service under a special court order.

Whoever serves the notice files a return of service. When service reaches a person fewer than 30 days before the date, the notice counts as timely only if the sale is continued to a date at least 30 days after the last required service.

What is an Act 91 notice, and what is HEMAP?

Act 91 of 1983 created the Homeowners' Emergency Mortgage Assistance Program, run by the Pennsylvania Housing Finance Agency. It is a loan program for owners facing foreclosure through no fault of their own. It is not a grant, and the funds must be repaid.

  • The home must be in Pennsylvania, owner-occupied, and a one- or two-family residence.
  • The owner must be at least 60 days behind and must have received an Act 91 Notice from the lender.
  • FHA Title II purchase mortgages are not eligible.
  • A loan is capped at 24 or 36 months of delinquency or $60,000, whichever comes first.
  • The minimum monthly payment set by law is $25 per mortgage assisted.

The clock is short. A face-to-face meeting with an approved counseling agency must happen within 33 days of the notice date, the agency must send the application to PHFA within 30 days of that meeting, and PHFA decides within 60 days of receiving it. Foreclosure actions pause while those time limits are met. The counselor will ask for a letter explaining the hardship, the Act 91 Notice, photo identification, three recent pay stubs, three years of federal tax returns, the deed, and monthly statements for loans and charge accounts. A denial can be appealed in writing, postmarked within 15 days of the denial letter. The HEMAP office is at 717-780-3940 or 1-800-342-2397.

Can a court set aside the sale?

Yes, but only on a petition filed in time. Rule 3132 lets the court, on petition of a party in interest and for proper cause, set aside the sale and order a resale before the sheriff's deed is delivered.

The sheriff executes the deed no sooner than 20 days and no later than 40 days after the schedule of distribution is filed, or after the sale if no schedule is needed, provided no petition to set the sale aside is pending. Rule 3135 also lets a purchaser ask the court to correct a defective deed, and it gives a plaintiff or purchaser a path to divest a junior lienholder who never received notice.

Does the sale wipe out what I owe?

Not always. When the lender buys the house at the sale for less than the judgment, 42 Pa.C.S. 8103 requires the lender to petition the court to fix the property's fair market value before collecting any balance. The debtor is then released to the extent of that value, less prior liens, costs and taxes not discharged by the sale.

If the lender fails to file within the six-month period in section 5522, the debtor or another person bound by the judgment may petition to have the judgment marked satisfied. The statute also voids any agreement to waive these protections. A debtor or owner who was never named or served in the valuation petition is discharged from personal liability on that debt.

Who is paid from the sale proceeds?

The sheriff files a schedule of distribution that shows how the money will be split among the parties with claims. Under the handbill language in Rule 3129.2, that schedule is filed no later than 30 days after the sale, and distribution follows it unless someone files exceptions within ten days after filing.

That ten-day window matters to owners with surplus money, to junior lienholders and to anyone else who thinks the numbers are wrong. Check the sheriff's office for the filing date, since the handbill states the date the sheriff chose.

Is transfer tax due on a foreclosure sale?

Generally no. Under 61 Pa. Code 91.193, transfers made under a mortgage foreclosure action, and transfers in a judicial sale for tax collection, are excluded from realty transfer tax. So is a deed in lieu of foreclosure to the mortgage holder, if the statement of value shows where the mortgage is recorded. The deed-in-lieu exclusion does not extend to someone who buys or is assigned the lender's bid.

Can I sell the house before the sheriff sale date?

Yes, an owner can sell before the sale takes place, and a closing that pays the lender in full removes the reason for the sale. Ask the lender or its attorney for a written payoff figure that includes legal costs, and give your buyer's title company that number so the closing date stays ahead of the sheriff's date.

Check the handbill and the written notice for the exact date. A sale can be continued, so confirm the current date with the county sheriff's office before you commit to a closing schedule. The county's Prothonotary or sheriff can tell you where the case stands.

How much notice does an owner get before a sheriff sale?

At least 30 days. The sheriff posts handbills 30 days ahead, the plaintiff serves written notice 30 days ahead, and newspaper publication starts at least 21 days before the sale.

Can the lender and I still work something out after the notice?

Yes. HEMAP exists for exactly this, and an application started within the 33-day window pauses the foreclosure while the time limits are met. Ask your lender about other options too.

How long after the sale is the sheriff's deed delivered?

The sheriff delivers the deed no sooner than 20 days and no later than 40 days after the schedule of distribution or the sale, unless a petition to set the sale aside has been filed.

Can a lender chase me for money after the sale?

Only after it petitions the court to fix fair market value under 42 Pa.C.S. 8103. You are credited with that value against the debt, and if the lender misses the six-month deadline you may ask the court to mark the judgment satisfied.

Who holds the sale?

The county sheriff. The sheriff of the county where the property sits posts the handbills and publishes the notice of sale.

What closing costs does a Pennsylvania home seller face?

The one charge written into Pennsylvania law for nearly every deed is the realty transfer tax, and it is usually the largest line a seller can predict in advance. Other charges, such as a loan payoff, agent compensation and title work, depend on your contract and your lender, so ask your settlement agent for a written estimate before you sign.

The Department of Revenue describes the state tax as 1 percent of the value of the real estate, including improvements contracted for, transferred by deed, instrument, long-term lease or other writing. County recorders of deeds collect it at recording, usually together with a local transfer tax set by the school district and municipality. That local piece is why a closing in one Pennsylvania town can cost far more in transfer tax than a closing in the next county over.

  • State realty transfer tax: 1 percent of value.
  • Local realty transfer tax: set by the municipality and school district, so it varies by address.
  • Recording fees: paid to the county, and in Allegheny County by a separate check from the transfer tax.

How much is the Pennsylvania realty transfer tax by place?

The combined rate turns on the property's location. Allegheny County says its transfer tax ranges from 2 percent to 5 percent of the total consideration, with 1 percent going to the state and the rest to the municipality and school district. Philadelphia lists 3.578 percent for the City plus 1 percent for the Commonwealth, a total of 4.578 percent.

The Allegheny County Real Estate Division publishes worked examples that show how the pieces stack. A $40,000 house in Shaler Township carries a 2 percent total, while the same price inside the City of Pittsburgh carries 5 percent. For a house elsewhere in the state, ask the county recorder of deeds for the municipality and school district rates that apply to the parcel.

School district0.5% ($200)1% ($400)
Total2% ($800)5% ($2,000)

Who pays the transfer tax, the buyer or the seller?

Both sides are legally on the hook, and the contract decides who actually writes the check. Under 61 Pa. Code 91.111, paying the tax is the joint and several duty of the parties, and they may split it as they agree, though the Commonwealth keeps its rights against both.

Philadelphia describes the common habit directly: the tax is usually split evenly between buyer and seller, which is not a legal requirement. The City can collect 100 percent from either party, so a seller who agreed to pay half still has an interest in seeing the full amount paid at settlement. Read the transfer tax clause in your agreement of sale, because a buyer can offer to absorb it as part of negotiation.

What value is the tax calculated on?

In an ordinary arm's length sale, the tax base is the total agreed consideration paid or to be paid. Section 91.132 adds that liens existing before the transfer and not removed by it count toward value, whether or not the buyer assumes the debt.

Some transfers use a computed value instead. Under 61 Pa. Code 91.135 that covers foreclosure, judicial and tax sales, gifts or nominal-consideration transfers, exchanges for stock or partnership interests, and transactions that are not bona fide sales. Philadelphia explains the method: take the assessed value from the Office of Property Assessment, apply the common level ratio set each year by the State Tax Equalization Board, and multiply the result by the tax rate. Allegheny County notes that new common level ratio factors take effect each year on July 1.

Which transfers escape the tax?

Several categories are excluded, but the exclusion must be claimed on the paperwork. The Department of Revenue names certain transfers among family members, transfers to governmental units, between religious organizations, to shareholders or partners, and to or from nonprofit industrial development agencies, plus deeds to burial sites, certain farm and real estate company transfers, and property passed by will or intestate succession.

  • Spouses, parents and children, grandparents and grandchildren, and siblings fall within the family exclusion in 61 Pa. Code 91.193, and Philadelphia asks for documentation of the relationship.
  • A devise by will or under intestate law, made for no or nominal consideration, is not taxable, but a transfer under an option to purchase in a will is taxable.
  • Philadelphia says transfer tax is still due if mortgages, liens or debts on the property are not paid at the time of transfer.
  • A sale by an estate to a buyer is taxable. Philadelphia gives the example of property willed to several people and then sold to one of them.

What paperwork and deadlines go with the tax?

A statement of value, filed in duplicate with the deed, is the key form. It states the true, full and complete value and, if you claim an exclusion, the reason the document is not taxable. Section 91.112 lets the parties skip it when the deed itself states the full value and no exclusion is claimed, and a familial transfer can skip it if the deed clearly states the relationship. Allegheny County calls its version PA form REV-183.

Philadelphia says the tax is due when the document is presented for recording, and acquirers must pay within 30 days of acquiring the real estate. Misrepresenting the transaction or failing to record it can bring penalties of up to 50 percent of the tax due. Paying by mail there takes three certified checks: one to the Recorder of Deeds, one to the City and one to the Commonwealth. In Allegheny County, expect one check for transfer tax and a separate one for recording fees.

How does this apply to an inherited or as-is Pennsylvania house?

A house you inherit can pass to you without transfer tax, but selling it afterward is an ordinary taxable sale. The exclusion in 91.159 covers the devise itself, not a later deed from you to a purchaser, so plan for the full state and local rate at closing unless another exclusion fits.

If heirs divide property among themselves, 91.159 also treats a division in kind as taxable only to the extent someone takes more than an undivided share, or pays consideration. A buyer who purchases an as-is, tenant-occupied or repair-heavy house pays the same percentage as any other buyer, because the tax follows the price and the liens, not the condition. Ask the county recorder of deeds for the current local rate before you agree on a net figure.

Frequently asked questions

Does Pennsylvania charge a state transfer tax on every home sale?

Yes, the state tax is 1 percent of the value of the real estate, unless the transfer is excluded. Excluded transfers include certain family transfers and property passed by will or intestate succession, and the exclusion has to be claimed on the filing.

Is the Philadelphia transfer tax higher than the rest of Pennsylvania?

Philadelphia lists 4.578 percent in total, made up of 3.578 percent for the City and 1 percent for the Commonwealth. Allegheny County reports a range of 2 percent to 5 percent, so the City of Pittsburgh reaches the top of that range while smaller municipalities sit lower.

Can the buyer pay the whole transfer tax?

Yes, the parties may agree on who pays under 61 Pa. Code 91.111. The Commonwealth keeps its rights against both parties, so the deal terms in your contract with the buyer do not remove the seller's legal exposure if the tax goes unpaid.

Do liens on the house raise the taxable value?

Yes, in a bona fide sale the value includes liens that existed before the transfer and were not removed by it, whether or not the buyer assumes the underlying debt. Liens paid off at closing do not add to the value.

Where do I find the local rate for my address?

Call the recorder of deeds for your house's county. That office collects the state tax and the local tax together at recording and can name the municipal and school district rates for the parcel.

How does probate work in Pennsylvania?

Probate in Pennsylvania runs through the Register of Wills in the county where the decedent had a last family or principal residence. That office grants letters, which are the court-recognized proof that one person may act for the estate. Disputes and sale approvals go to the orphans' court division of the same county.

For a house, letters are the first gate. Without them, nobody can sign a deed for the estate, and a title company will not insure a buyer. The rules sit in Title 20 of the Pennsylvania Consolidated Statutes, which is the Probate, Estates and Fiduciaries Code. This page follows that title from the petition through the sale of the house and the distribution of proceeds.

Which county's Register of Wills handles the estate?

Section 3151 says letters for a Pennsylvania domiciliary are granted only by the register of the county where the decedent had a last family or principal residence. A decedent who lived in Erie County and owned a second house elsewhere is still probated in Erie County. If the decedent was domiciled outside Pennsylvania, any county where estate property sits may grant the letters, and those letters are then exclusive across the Commonwealth.

The petition must be sworn. Section 3153 requires the decedent's name, age, domicile, last residence and date and place of death, the heirs where there is no will, and the estimated value of personal property plus the estimated value and location of real property in Pennsylvania. Expect the house address to appear on the petition itself.

Who gets letters, and in what order?

If the will names an executor, section 3155(a) directs the register to grant letters testamentary to that person, even if the executor has declined a trust under the will. With no will, or no executor who acts, letters of administration go to a person in a priority list.

Priority for letters of administration under 20 Pa.C.S. 3155(b)
OrderPerson
1Those entitled to the residuary estate under the will
2The surviving spouse
3Intestate heirs, with preference by size of share
4Principal creditors of the decedent
5Other fit persons

A person who renounces may name a nominee, in the register's discretion. Section 3155(c) adds a waiting period: letters for creditors and other fit persons cannot issue until 30 days after death unless the higher-ranking persons consent.

Can a house skip probate through the small estate process?

Usually not, because the small estate petition in section 3102 excludes real estate from the $50,000 figure. The court may direct distribution of personal property up to $50,000 in gross value, and the court's authority is not restricted because the decedent owned real estate. But that process distributes personal property. A house still needs a person with authority to convey it.

Section 3101 gives other shortcuts that never reach real estate. An employer may pay up to $10,000 in wages or benefits to a spouse, child, parent, sibling in that order of preference, whether or not a representative has been appointed. Neither shortcut replaces letters when the house must be sold.

What can the personal representative do with the real estate?

The representative has the right to take possession of, maintain and administer the decedent's real and personal estate, with one exception: real estate occupied at death by an heir or devisee with the decedent's consent. Under section 3311, the representative collects rents and income until the property is sold or distributed, and makes reasonable expenditures to preserve it. The same section says nothing limits the power to sell real estate occupied by an heir or devisee.

For sale, the powers in section 3351 are broad. Unless the will says otherwise, the representative may sell at public or private sale any real property not specifically devised, and may sell specifically devised property with the devisee's joinder. If the will withholds the power, or a judicial sale effect is advisable, section 3353 requires an order of the orphans' court division. Section 3357 then passes the decedent's full title to the buyer, discharged from legacy liens and estate debts, provided any required bond was given.

  • No will power to sell: ask the court for a section 3353 order.
  • House specifically left to one person: that person joins the deed.
  • Heir living in the house: the representative can still sell it.

What happens to a vacant or burdened house during probate?

The representative carries the duty to maintain the house, because section 3311 makes preservation of estate property part of the job. The statute calls for reasonable expenditures necessary to preserve it. Heirs who live far away often find the first months of probate expensive for exactly this reason.

Section 3312 gives one pressure valve. When property is of no value to the estate, the court may authorize the representative to renounce the right to administer it. A house with debts above its worth can fall into that category, though the court decides, and an attorney should advise before anyone asks.

Real estate taxes also continue. Under 53 Pa.C.S. 8863, property of a decedent's estate may be assessed in the name of the decedent or the personal representative, so tax bills may still arrive in the decedent's name. Ask the county assessment office to update the mailing address once letters issue.

What must be advertised, filed and paid before distributing sale proceeds?

The representative must advertise the grant of letters in one newspaper of general circulation near the decedent's residence and in the legal periodical designated by court rule, once a week for three successive weeks. Section 3162 requires the notice to invite claims and ask debtors to pay. This advertisement starts a clock in section 3532: a representative who distributes at their own risk, without an audit, is free of liability to a claimant unless the claim became known within one year after the first complete advertisement, or later but before distribution.

The inventory is due under section 3301(c) by the date the account is filed or the inheritance tax return is due, whichever is earlier, and any party in interest may demand an earlier filing. Inheritance tax is delinquent nine months after death, with a 5 percent discount if paid within three months, per the Department of Revenue.

How does a cash sale fit into probate?

A cash sale can close as soon as letters exist and the title company is satisfied with the signing authority. The estate avoids months of repairs, staging and listing, and stops paying carrying costs on an empty house. The representative still handles the inheritance tax, advertisement and accounting.

Bring the letters, the will if there is one, the death certificate and any court order to the title company, and ask which documents it requires from the Register of Wills. If an heir lives in the house, plan a move-out date in writing before the closing.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need probate to sell a house in Pennsylvania?

Yes, in most cases. The small estate process covers personal property only, so a house needs a personal representative holding letters from the Register of Wills.

Which county do I file in?

File in the county where the decedent had a last family or principal residence. Section 3151 says letters for a Pennsylvania domiciliary are granted only by that county's register.

Can an heir living in the house be forced out for the sale?

The representative's power to sell is not limited because an heir or devisee lives there. How to end the occupancy is a question for the orphans' court or an attorney, and a written move-out date helps.

How long are creditors given to make a claim?

A representative who distributes at their own risk is protected against claims unknown within one year after the first complete advertisement of letters, or later but before distribution. The advertisement runs once a week for three weeks.

What happens if there is no will and no relatives?

Under a change effective January 16, 2026, the estate goes first to an endowed community fund in the decedent's municipality, then school district, then county, and only then to the Commonwealth.

How does a Pennsylvania tax sale work?

A Pennsylvania tax sale is a forced sale of real estate to collect unpaid real estate tax. Outside the first and second class counties, a county tax claim bureau runs it under the Real Estate Tax Sale Law, published by the legislature as Act 542 of 1947. Philadelphia, the only first class county, follows a different statute and court process, covered further down.

Under the 1947 law, a tax claim is a first lien on the parcel. The bureau gives the owner a one-year window to pay, then offers the property at an upset sale, and then, if no one bids the full upset price, can ask the court of common pleas for a judicial sale. Each step carries its own notice rules, and a defect in notice is the most common ground for an owner to object.

The upset price is the total the bureau must recover. It adds the Commonwealth tax liens, the claim being sold on, any other tax claims or judgments, current-year taxes, municipal claims such as water or sewer, and the record and sale costs (section 605). That is why a house with a small tax debt can still carry an upset price well above the original bill.

Which law applies in Philadelphia and which in the rest of the state?

The 1947 Real Estate Tax Sale Law covers counties other than the first and second class, and Philadelphia is the state's only first class county. Philadelphia instead uses the Municipal Claim and Tax Lien Law of 1923 (Act 153), which sends delinquent accounts through the Court of Common Pleas and the Sheriff's Office.

  • Tax claim bureau counties: a September upset sale, no redemption after the sale, and a deed from the bureau to the buyer.
  • Philadelphia: a petition and court order, a sheriff's auction, and a nine month redemption period after the sheriff's deed is acknowledged for most homes.
  • A judicial sale under either system clears the taxing bodies' liens, while the 1947 law lets recorded mortgages and ground rents survive an upset sale unless they were part of the upset price.

What are the steps and dates in a tax claim bureau sale?

The calendar is fixed by statute, so an owner who tracks it can usually see the sale coming a year ahead. The table lists the main steps in order.

Tax claim bureau sale steps under Act 542 of 1947 (section numbers refer to the Act)
StepRuleSection
Notice of claimMailed by July 31 each year; a one-year discharge period starts July 1308

Published and mailed noticeAt least 30 days before the sale, by newspaper and certified mail; posting at least 10 days before602
Owner-occupied homesPersonal service by the sheriff or an appointee at least 10 days before the sale601(a)(3)
Return to courtConsolidated return within 60 days; owner objections within 30 days after confirmation nisi607

Source: Pennsylvania General Assembly text of the Real Estate Tax Sale Law.

How can an owner stop a tax sale before it happens?

An owner can stop the sale by paying, by signing a payment agreement, or by selling the house and paying the bureau from the closing proceeds. The options the statute names are:

  • Pay in full before July 1 of the year after the notice of claim, which also keeps the address out of the advertisement. Paying after July 1 but before the sale still stops it, though the property may appear in the printed list (section 501).
  • Sign a stay agreement with the bureau before the sale: 25 percent of the amount due up front and the balance in no more than three installments within one year (section 603). Missing a payment lets the bureau proceed at a sale held at least 90 days after the default.
  • Ask for an extension of up to 12 more months for owner-occupied real estate, if the county commissioners have adopted that program. The schedule must have at least four payments, with a first payment no larger than 25 percent (sections 502.1 and 503.1).
  • Ask about deferral if every owner-occupant is 65 or older and household income falls within the state rent rebate limit, where the county has adopted it (section 504).

The discharge certificate the bureau issues after payment records the satisfaction, and the bureau must forward collected money to the taxing districts at least every three months (section 501).

What happens to the title after an upset sale?

The title passes to the buyer once the court confirms the sale and the buyer pays the bid, and the owner has no right to redeem after the actual sale (section 501(c)). The bureau signs a fee simple deed as trustee, and the buyer pays to record it (section 608).

An upset sale conveys title subject to recorded mortgages, claims, ground rents and Commonwealth tax liens that were not included in the upset price (section 609). A judicial sale is stronger: the court orders the property sold free and clear of tax claims, mortgages and liens, other than separately taxed ground rents, and the leftover proceeds go to the office the commissioners designate (section 612).

An owner cannot buy the property back at a judicial sale, a private sale or from the repository for unsold property (section 618(a)). The one opening is narrow: if a property stays unsold after the upset sale and still sits on the bureau docket, the bureau may accept full payment of all returned taxes, costs, penalties and interest, but not installments (section 618(a.1)). A landlord whose rental license a municipality revoked cannot bid at the sale (section 601(d)).

How is a Philadelphia sheriff sale different?

In Philadelphia the City petitions the court to foreclose on a tax or other municipal lien, and the court orders a sale at a sheriff's auction. The City's Department of Revenue sends a warning of risk of tax foreclosure to qualifying accounts that owe and have no payment agreement. Online bidding for sheriff sales runs through Bid4Assets.com/Philadelphia, which the Sheriff's Office launched as its auction search platform in October 2026.

The 1923 statute gives the owner of a property sold on a tax or municipal claim nine months from the acknowledgment of the sheriff's deed to redeem by paying the bid, deed costs, taxes paid, other charges, and interest at 10 percent a year (section 32(a)). A vacant property carries no redemption right, and a home counts as occupied only if one individual or family lived there continuously for at least 90 days before the sale and still does when the deed is acknowledged (section 32(c)).

Philadelphia also offers the Owner-occupied Payment Agreement, which can set payments as low as $0 a month for some owners. The City's guidance is to contact the Department of Revenue, or the law firm named in the notice, as soon as a tax sale notice arrives.

Can I sell a house that is headed for a tax sale?

Yes. An owner can sell at any point before the actual sale, and the unpaid tax, interest and costs come out of the seller's side of the closing. The practical limit is time, because the buyer must close and the bureau must receive payoff funds before the sale date.

  • Ask the county tax claim bureau for a written payoff that includes the claim, interest, other tax claims, accrued current taxes and record costs.
  • Give that figure to the closing agent so it is paid from the seller's proceeds and the bureau issues its certificate of discharge.
  • Check for municipal claims, such as water and sewer, that sit outside the bureau's tax claim but still ride along in the upset price.
  • In Philadelphia, request a water payoff at least 30 days before settlement and ask the Department of Revenue for the real estate tax balance.

A seller who is short on time can ask a cash buyer to close quickly, as long as the payoff and the deed recording fit inside the sale calendar.

Frequently asked questions

Can I get my house back after a Pennsylvania tax sale?

In a county run by a tax claim bureau, no. The statute says there is no redemption after the actual sale, and an owner cannot buy the property back at a judicial or private sale. Philadelphia is the exception, where an owner of an occupied home can petition to redeem within nine months after the sheriff's deed is acknowledged.

When is the Pennsylvania upset sale held?

The bureau sets it no earlier than the second Monday of September and before October 1, and it may be adjourned or continued. If the sale is held by the end of the calendar year, no new notice is needed. Ask the county tax claim bureau for its published date.

How much notice must the owner get?

Notice comes in several forms. The bureau publishes the sale and mails certified notice at least 30 days ahead, posts the property at least 10 days ahead, and serves an owner-occupant personally at least 10 days ahead. An owner who objects after the sale has 30 days from confirmation nisi to file.

What does a payment agreement require?

A stay agreement under section 603 requires 25 percent of the total due and the rest in no more than three installments inside one year. A default lets the bureau list the property again at a sale held at least 90 days later.

Does selling the house before the sale clear the tax debt?

Yes, if the closing pays the full payoff. The bureau applies the money to the claim, issues a certificate of discharge and removes the property from the sale list. Ask the bureau for the exact figure, since interest and costs change as the sale date nears.
